easy.explanation: Isaiah begins by saying, “Howl, ye ships of Tarshish.”
easy.q: Who is told to howl at the beginning of the passage?

easy.explanation: Tyre is described as “a mart of nations.”
easy.q: Which city is described as a mart of nations?

easy.explanation: The merchants of Zidon are said to pass over the sea.
easy.q: Who is mentioned as passing over the sea as a merchant?

answers: They moved their work onto the land
Their harbor activity and commerce were disrupted
medium.explanation: Tyre was laid waste, leaving no house and no entering in for the ships.
medium.q: What happened to the ships’ activity after Tyre was laid waste?

medium.explanation: The passage calls the seed of Sihor and the harvest of the river Tyre’s revenue.
medium.q: What did Egypt provide to Tyre through the sea?

medium.explanation: “Howl” is a call to mourn because of Tyre’s destruction.
medium.q: What does “Howl” mean in this passage?

answers: Egypt was protected by Tyre’s army
Egypt received military help from Tyre
Egypt’s produce and sea trade were connected with Tyre
challenge.explanation: Tyre’s commerce was supplied by Egypt’s harvest through the sea.
challenge.q: Why would Egypt be greatly pained by the report of Tyre?

answers: A busy commercial center becomes a ruined and silent city
A land city becomes a desert city
A poor city becomes a wealthy city
challenge.explanation: Tyre had been a mart of nations, but it is then described as laid waste.
challenge.q: What central contrast appears in the description of Tyre?

answers: They had gone to war together
challenge.explanation: The passage links their trade and mourning, showing that Tyre’s fall affected the wider region.
challenge.q: What does the mention of Tyre, Zidon, and Egypt together suggest?

paragraphs.title: Tyre’s Destruction and the Exile of Its People

easy.explanation: The passage says, “Pass ye over to Tarshish.”
easy.q: Where are the inhabitants of the isle told to go?

easy.explanation: The Lord purposes to stain its pride, bring its honorable people into contempt, and destroy its strongholds.
easy.q: What does Tyre lose because of the judgment against it?

easy.explanation: The text says, “The Lord of hosts hath purposed it.”
easy.q: Who purposed the destruction of Tyre?

answers: Their city and strongholds have been brought down
They are searching for harvests in Egypt
The sea has been closed to them
medium.explanation: The destruction of Tyre’s strength causes its people to leave and sojourn elsewhere.
medium.q: Why do the people of Tyre wander according to the passage?

medium.explanation: Strong holds are fortified places that provide defense and security.
medium.q: What does “strong holds” mean in this passage?

answers: The Lord purposes to humble its pride
Its pride protects it from its enemies
Its pride causes its trade to increase
medium.explanation: The Lord purposes to stain the pride of all glory and bring the honorable into contempt.
medium.q: What is the relationship between Tyre’s pride and its destruction?

answers: The exiles will immediately find rest there
Their wandering will continue without secure rest
They will quickly return to Tyre
challenge.explanation: The passage says that even in Chittim they will have no rest.
challenge.q: What does the command to pass over to Chittim emphasize?

answers: As an ancient city once known for joy and prosperity
As a city that had never been inhabited
As a city built after its destruction
challenge.explanation: Tyre is called a joyous city whose antiquity is of ancient days.
challenge.q: How is Tyre characterized in the question, “Is this your joyous city”?

challenge.explanation: The Lord judges Tyre’s pride, destroys its strongholds, and sends its people away.
challenge.q: What is the main sequence of events in these verses?

paragraphs.title: Babylon as the Destroyer of Tyre

easy.explanation: Isaiah says, “Behold the land of the Chaldeans.”
easy.q: Which land is described in connection with the destroying power?

answers: Founded them and raised up towers and palaces
easy.explanation: The Assyrian founded the people and they set up towers and raised palaces.
easy.q: What did the Assyrian do for the people of that land?

answers: Their strength has been laid waste
easy.explanation: The ships are told to howl because their strength has been laid waste.
easy.q: Why are the ships of Tarshish told to howl at the end of the passage?

answers: A people not previously established becomes a destructive power
A great empire becomes a people without a land
Sea merchants become builders of palaces
medium.explanation: The passage says this people was not until the Assyrian founded it, yet it brought Tyre to ruin.
medium.q: What change is described concerning the land of the Chaldeans?

medium.explanation: The verse says, “he brought it to ruin.”
medium.q: What was the result of the Chaldeans’ action against Tyre?

answers: Their source of security and power is destroyed
medium.explanation: The ships’ strength represents the power and security associated with Tyre.
medium.q: What does “your strength is laid waste” mean for the ships of Tarshish?

answers: In both places the ships are told to howl because of Tyre’s fall
In both places the ships are told to sail to Egypt
In both places Tyre is described as being rebuilt
challenge.explanation: The chapter begins and ends with a call for the ships of Tarshish to howl.
challenge.q: How does verse 14 connect with the beginning of Isaiah 23?

answers: Destruction depends only on the size of an army
A seemingly insignificant people can become the destroyer of a commercial power
challenge.explanation: Though the people was not previously established, it became an instrument of Tyre’s ruin.
challenge.q: What does the contrast between the former condition of the Chaldeans and their later action emphasize?

answers: Tyre’s destruction leads to the loss of the ships’ strength
The ships’ trade leads to the building of Tyre
challenge.explanation: After Tyre is brought to ruin, the ships are told that their strength is laid waste.
challenge.q: What cause-and-effect relationship appears in these verses?

paragraphs.title: Seventy Years of Oblivion and the Consecration of Trade

easy.explanation: The passage says Tyre shall be forgotten seventy years.
easy.q: How long will Tyre be forgotten?

answers: It will return to commercial activity
It will disappear from the earth
easy.explanation: After seventy years, the Lord will visit Tyre and it will return to its trade.
easy.q: What will happen to Tyre after the seventy years?

answers: Those who dwell before the Lord
easy.explanation: The merchandise shall be for them that dwell before the Lord.
easy.q: For whom will Tyre’s merchandise ultimately be used?

answers: As a song of praise for a righteous queen
In the figurative language of a harlot seeking customers
medium.explanation: Tyre is told to take a harp and sing as a harlot who has been forgotten.
medium.q: How is Tyre’s return to commerce described?

answers: Payment or profit gained from activity
medium.explanation: “Hire” refers to the income or profit gained through Tyre’s commerce.
medium.q: What does “hire” mean in this passage?

answers: Food to eat sufficiently and durable clothing
Ships to be sent to Egypt
medium.explanation: The merchandise will provide food and durable clothing for those who dwell before the Lord.
medium.q: What will Tyre’s merchandise provide according to the last verse?

answers: Commerce returns, but its final use is dedicated to the Lord’s people
challenge.explanation: Tyre returns to trade, but its merchandise becomes holiness to the Lord.
challenge.q: What is the central change in Tyre’s commercial status at the end of the passage?

answers: A long period of forgetting followed by a change in Tyre’s condition
The time required to build Tyre’s walls
challenge.explanation: The seventy years mark Tyre’s prolonged forgetting before its restoration to trade.
challenge.q: What does the period of seventy years emphasize?

answers: After being forgotten, Tyre sings so that it may be remembered
Because it is forgotten, Tyre can never trade again
Tyre is remembered immediately and never experiences judgment
challenge.explanation: Tyre is told to sing many songs so that it may be remembered after the seventy years.
challenge.q: What relationship exists between Tyre’s being forgotten and its being remembered?
